items.quote: it is repugnant neither to Nature nor Reason that a Man may prolong his life beyond the common ordinary age of Men, even to a long time, and that for two Reasons
items.note: Croll holds that lengthening life past the ordinary age agrees with Nature and Reason, and announces two reasons; he grants it may pass for the talk of Vaine men.

items.quote: Porta reject the opinion of those that cast mens fortune from the day or houre of their nativity prefixing the bounds of life
items.name: Porta
items.note: The margin note gives Porta as rejecting those who fix the bounds of life from the day or hour of birth, and as saying that one wary of his infirmities may live longer.

items.quote: Parac. chap. 7. of the Labyrinth of Physitians.
items.name: Parac.
items.note: The margin note names a chapter of a writing of Parac. beside the statement that life may be prolonged.

items.quote: in NATURALS there is no certaine appointed Terme apparent what day we shall die, but it is in our own hand and power to put an end to our life if we will, and to prolong it
items.note: First reason: in natural things no appointed day of death is apparent; ending or prolonging life lies in our own power, and prolonging it is said to be without offence to GOD.

items.quote: I speak here Phylosophically of the Naturall death
items.note: Croll says in which sense his words are meant here: Phylosophically, of the Naturall death, and not Theologically of the Fatall death.

items.quote: the Naturall death, which is onely the wasting of the Naturall Moysture and Heat, as may be seen in a burning lamp
items.note: The text says what Naturall death is: the wasting of the Naturall Moysture and Heat, likened to a burning lamp.

items.quote: the Fatall death and utmost Terme which God hath prefixt to every one, by which we are inforc'd not onely to pay the debt of Nature, but are compel'd also to undergoe the punishment for sin
items.note: The text says what the Fatall death is: the utmost Terme God has prefixed to every one, by which the debt of Nature is paid and the punishment for sin undergone.

items.quote: Death is the Bound which we cannot passe, nor is there any day or hour, for by the Grace of God we live the Terme without houres.
items.note: Death is a bound that cannot be passed, yet no day or hour is set; we live the Terme without houres.

items.quote: As God hath numbred our hairs, so also doth he reckon our years, leaving them in our power
items.note: God reckons our years and leaves them in our power.

items.quote: a long and lasting life of Man in this world is not displeasing to him, especially if it be spent in the Fear and Service of his Creator
items.note: A long life does not displease God, the more so if spent in his fear and service; the text draws this from God's pleasure that Man should live for ever and from the propagation of Mankind.

items.quote: that utmost and fixed Terme or determined poynt of DIVINE PREDESTINATION which is unknown to mortalls
items.note: The fixed Terme of DIVINE PREDESTINATION is said to be unknown to mortals; a long life always stays short of it.

items.quote: imposed on our first Parents and their heires, for their Fall from Originall Righteousnesse, beyond which Bound no man can goe.
items.note: The fixed Terme was imposed on the first Parents and their heirs for their Fall; no man can go beyond it.

items.quote: See Paracelsus of long life.
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The margin note points to a writing of Paracelsus beside the passage on the fixed Terme unknown to mortals.

items.quote: See Paracelsus in lib. 8.
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The margin note points to Paracelsus, lib. 8, beside the statement that no man can go beyond the Bound; the note does not say of which writing.

items.quote: utmost and fixed Terme or determined poynt
items.note: The same paragraph says there is no certaine appointed Terme apparent and no day or hour, and also speaks of a fixed Terme or determined point. The paragraph itself sets the two apart as the Naturall death and the Fatall death, and calls the fixed Terme unknown to mortals.

items.quote: so may he prolong his life by removing these impediments, so that at last he may attaine to the appointed Terme of the Nature of life.
items.note: As diseases may shorten a man's time before the appointed Terme, so removing these impediments prolongs life until the appointed Terme of the Nature of life is reached.

items.quote: Archid. of the Elixirs.
items.name: Archid. of the Elixirs
items.note: The margin note names a writing beside the statement that life is compassed about with diseases.

items.quote: It is the conservation of the Human body from all accidentall corruption.
items.note: The note says of something that it is the conservation of the human body from all accidental corruption; the note does not name what 'It' is, and it follows the words 'of the Elixirs'.

items.quote: There is a two fold death, from the Iliad or first principle, and from the Ens or Being.
items.what: a two fold death, from the Iliad or first principle, and from the Ens or Being
items.note: The note sets apart two deaths and glosses its two words: Iliad as first principle, Ens as Being.

items.quote: The Soule of perpetuity or the Spirit of Light joyned to Nature with the light is perpetuall, and will not suffer such a conjunction and such a life to be short.
items.note: The note says the Soule of perpetuity or Spirit of Light, joined to Nature, is perpetual and does not let such a life be short. The note also calls death Gods minister that expecteth our intestine war.

items.quote: the aforesaid Medicine
items.note: The Medicine is called aforesaid: the text points back to an earlier place in this writing; the lines given do not show which.

items.quote: God hath created the aforesaid Medicine for the preservation of life, which may preserve our body as well from the corruption of our Parents, as from the defect of our own government
items.note: Second reason: God created the Medicine to preserve life; it keeps the body from inherited corruption and from faults of our own government, cures infirmities, repairs what is wasted and chases away the diseases that cause the naturall death.

items.quote: ultimate death the most Terrible of all Terrible things (which is the destruction of the Mummy) which God the most high Creator hath ordained as the wages of sinners
items.note: The text says what ultimate death is: the destruction of the Mummy, ordained by God as the wages of sinners. The Medicine works until this death.

items.quote: Paracelsus saith that the death which is from the resolution of the Iliad may be hindred by the industry of the Physitian, but that which is from the Ens or Being cannot
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: Paracelsus is given as saying that the death from the resolution of the Iliad can be hindered by the physician, the death from the Ens or Being cannot.

items.quote: as we may preserve a little fire by laying on more wood; so also may our life be prolonged by administring such Remedies and secrets as are derived from the fountaine of Gods gifts
items.note: Life is prolonged by Remedies and secrets as a small fire is kept by adding wood. The words follow 'Paracelsus saith' after a colon; the text does not show whether they are still his or Croll's own.

items.quote: we being destitute of wisdome know not that wood wherewith our life might be cherished and prolonged
items.note: 'wood' is used here in a second sense, carried over from the fire comparison just before: the thing by which life is cherished and prolonged. The text says we lack the wisdom to know it.

items.quote: did attaine to so many ages, not by Nature and property of Time, for then all had been Long-liv'd, but by the help of Secrets and by Wisdome which was revealed but to few
items.note: Adam and many of his time reached their great ages not by Nature or the property of the time, but by Secrets and Wisdome; they are also said to have lived a more frugall life than we.

items.quote: by Wisdome which was revealed but to few, and by speciall knowledge which God gave them in this particular
items.note: The wisdom that lengthened life was revealed to few only, as a special knowledge given by God.

items.quote: Many holy men used this universall Medicine before the flood, which Adam also had in his Family
items.note: The Medicine is named universall, and is said to have been used by many holy men before the flood and held in Adam's family.

items.quote: as Lactantius witnesseth
items.name: Lactantius
items.note: Lactantius is named as witness that the universall Medicine was used before the flood and that Adam had it in his family.

items.quote: which strengthneth the Internall Balsom, and like Fire congregateth Homogeneous things, and segregateth Heterogeneous, which are of a contrary nature
items.note: What the universall Medicine does: it strengthens the Internall Balsom and, like Fire, gathers like things and parts unlike ones.

items.quote: dream that the Deluge washed away the efficacy of fruits & of growing things, or that the power and strength of mens bodies was spoyled by the Water
items.name: their judgements, who being ignorant of the Mysteries of the Element of Water
items.note: A view of unnamed people, reported in order to reject it: that the Deluge took away the efficacy of growing things or the strength of men's bodies. Croll calls them ignorant of the Mysteries of the Element of Water.

items.quote: all things that grow by the benefit of Water do yet sprout and spring forth in the same vigour and with the same efficacy as they did in Adams time.
items.note: Growing things have the same vigour and efficacy now as in Adam's time.

items.quote: Wherefore we want nothing but the knowledge of Secrets, and their use.
items.note: What is lacking is only the knowledge of Secrets and of their use.

items.quote: the Flood did not wast the things that grow, but wash'd away our wisdome of knowing them
items.note: The Flood took away not the things that grow but the wisdom of knowing them.

items.quote: These most secret of secrets have ever been hid from the common sort of them that professe Phylosophy, and especially sincemen began to abuse Wisdome, using it to an ill end
items.note: The most secret of secrets are said to have always been hidden from the common sort of those who profess Phylosophy, the more so since men began to abuse Wisdome.

items.quote: wise men lived together in the Centre reserving wisdome among themselves, but banished those that had it not into the circumference
items.name: Paracels.
items.note: The margin note, signed Paracels., says that when men multiplied the wise kept wisdom among themselves in the Centre and banished those without it to the circumference. It stands beside the passage on growing things and the lost wisdom.

items.quote: as few reach the Naturall Terme, so also few have known the reason of prolonging the life
items.note: Few reach the Naturall Terme and few have known the reason of prolonging life.

items.quote: the life is broken off, or shortned, two manner of wayes
items.note: The text announces two ways in which life is broken off or shortened; CH6.73 and CH6.74 give them as First and Secondly.

items.quote: MENS & ENS abrumpunt nobis vitam.
items.note: A margin note in Latin at the head of the first of the two ways names MENS and ENS together; the paragraphs beside it name the two ways as the MIND (CH6.73) and PER ENTEM, the Being (CH6.74).

items.quote: by the MIND, whence arise mentall diseases which are invisible, and affect us in our Mind, as Inchantment, Imagination, Estimation, Influence; Superstition, all which proceed from a spirituall affection
items.note: The first way: by the MIND. The text names the mentall diseases as invisible and lists five, all from a spirituall affection.

items.quote: No corporall guard or shelter availeth any thing against such like violences, but onely Faith which is able to resist them
items.note: Nothing bodily guards against these; only Faith resists them.

items.quote: some other Magicall means is requisite against witchcrafts and to cure those that are bewitched, and though the cure be difficult, yet is it possible.
items.note: Besides Faith, some Magicall means is required against witchcrafts and for the bewitched; the cure is hard but possible.

items.quote: that the act of the imagination is immanent, and that one mans body cannot be altered by another mans imagination
items.name: what may be said
items.note: The margin note reports an objection, of no named speaker, and sets it aside with 'Notwithstanding': that imagination stays within and cannot alter another man's body.

items.quote: these diseases which only Adept Physitians know, are healed without the help of Natural Physick
items.note: The mental diseases are said to be known to Adept Physitians only, and healed without Natural Physick.

items.quote: in the minds of men there is a kind of a hidden Virtue, of changing, attracting, and binding that which it desireth either to attract, or change, or bind, or hinder
items.note: A hidden Virtue in men's minds changes, attracts and binds what it desires, most of all when set to work with the greatest excess of Imagination and Will.

items.quote: the Antipathicall Loadstone, which doth (as it were) bewitch spiritually and invisibly
items.note: 'bewitch' is marked by '(as it were)' as not meant plainly of the Loadstone; the loadstone is brought as a known case to make the mind's hidden Virtue no strange thing.

items.quote: these five supernatural mischiefs
items.note: The mental diseases are counted as five and called supernatural mischiefs that could suffocate our spirit.

items.quote: i. e. Inchantment, Imagination, Estimation, Influence, Superstition.
items.note: The margin note says which the five supernatural mischiefs are.

items.quote: their malignant Astra's must be averted by a supernaturall cure and magicall help into something else, without any prophanation of Gods Name
items.note: What is to be done against the five mischiefs: their malignant Astra's are turned away into something else by a supernatural cure and magical help, without profaning God's Name. The lines given do not say how.

items.quote: those diseases that proceed from the Mind require a mentall cure
items.note: Diseases from the Mind need a mentall cure.

items.quote: of which see more in Paracels. his Philosophia Sagaci
items.name: Paracels.
items.note: For more on the mentall cure the text sends the reader to a writing of Paracels. named Philosophia Sagaci.

items.quote: Godlinesse is the chiefest remedy, guard, and preservation against such like evills, for certainly the auxiliary hands of God are the best preservative in all diseases.
items.note: Godlinesse is the chief remedy against these evils, and God's help the best preservative in all diseases.

items.quote: by the Being, as by Entall or Corporall diseases
items.note: The second way, headed PER ENTEM, is said in English to be by the Being, that is by Entall or Corporall diseases. Margin note N312 beside it is two gaps in the transcription and cannot be read.

items.quote: many who live to eate onely, and prefer a voluptuous superfluity before the Naturall necessity which is content and satisfied with a little, have surfeted themselves to death, and found death in the pot
items.note: Many shorten life by excess in eating; natural necessity is content with little.

items.quote: Health is preserved by fastings, and a moderate Diet is the best Governance to prolong the life.
items.note: Fasting keeps health and a moderate Diet is the best Governance for prolonging life.

items.quote: this cure of the harmes of the Naturall members which come from the Ens or Being, is to be sought from Natural causes and means, to wit, from the Elements and hidden Secrets
items.note: The cure of bodily harms from the Ens or Being is to be sought from natural causes and means, named as the Elements and hidden Secrets.

items.quote: Corporall medicines doe no good to mentall or supernaturall distempers, nor can mentall medicines be profitable to bodily diseases.
items.note: Bodily medicines do nothing for mental or supernatural distempers, nor mental medicines for bodily diseases.

items.quote: all diseases require their own proper cure, and reject any other remedy
items.note: Here every disease needs its own proper cure and rejects any other, and CH6.73 says the mental diseases are healed without Natural Physick; CH6.71 speaks of one universall Medicine that may chase away all diseases which cause the naturall death. The lines given do not say how the two stand together.

items.quote: by many various accidents may we be hindred and kept from attaining to the Naturall Term of life, as Theophrastus in his Books very often observeth
items.name: Theophrastus
items.note: Theophrastus is named as often observing in his Books that corruption in the womb, in birth and education, and many accidents keep us from the Naturall Term of life.

items.quote: wander wider then the bounds of a Preface, I shall now draw to a conclusion
items.note: The text calls itself a Preface with bounds and announces its conclusion.

items.quote: I have inserted in their proper places in this Prolix and Admonitory Preface
items.note: Croll names the writing and says the gain of his labours, watchings, studies and peregrinations is set in its proper places within it.

items.quote: divine Misteries are far greater than to be set forth by the splendor of mans words
items.note: Divine Misteries are greater than man's words can set forth.

items.quote: so far as was lawfull, and so much as was allowable by God, have I imparted candidly from the intimate and inmost Armory or Treasury of my Heart
items.note: Croll says he has imparted only as far as was lawful and allowed by God, and as far as divine Minerva hath given leave: a stated limit on what is told.

items.quote: Read them over and over, & over again, and againe; I hope it shall not repent thee of thy paines.
items.note: The margin note tells the reader to read these things many times over.

items.quote: to the Children of Learning and Heirs of Wisdome, who with second thoughts which are the wisest, shall clearly and with a considerate judgement passe thorow these things with a pure Mind and tongue
items.note: The readers for whom it is imparted are named: the Children of Learning and Heirs of Wisdome, who go through these things with second thoughts and a pure mind.

items.quote: reading them over in the light of God, without any superfluity or diminution, by often reiterated and evident speculations
items.note: How the text asks to be read: in the light of God, adding and taking away nothing, with often repeated consideration.

items.quote: but it concerns the publick good to make known also in publick writing what belongs to the publick, not out of pride or vaine glory, but moved with a desire of doing good
items.note: It is not enough to know for oneself; what belongs to the public should be made known in public writing, for posterity's instruction and the honour of God's bounty.

items.quote: We ought not to prefer our private profit before the publick good.
items.note: The margin note states the rule of public good before private profit.

items.quote: at this time I see it taught in publick Schools for the most part rather for the glory of Education, than the good and profit of the Auditors
items.note: One of his reasons for publishing: in the public Schools it is taught mostly for the glory of Education, not for the hearers' good.

items.quote: The School of Physick is not covered with tile, but with the Firmament:
items.note: The margin note says the School of Physick has the Firmament, not tile, for its roof.

items.quote: I lived freely to the great advantage of my studies above ten years in two of the very best and most honourable Families
items.note: Croll's statement about himself: more than ten years of free study in two families, which he ascribes to the assistance of the divine Majesty.

items.quote: in that of ESNE at Lyons in France, and in that of BAPPENHEIMIE in the Segniory of Mareschall
items.note: The two families are named. He says he instructed the noble offspring entrusted to him and travelled, in particular with MAXIMILIAN, whose father Conradus was then a prisoner in Mareschal.

items.quote: that Physitian that walketh according to the mind of Paracelsus is onely able to open the Book of Nature
items.note: The margin note says only the physician who follows the mind of Paracelsus can open the Book of Nature.

items.quote: I had special and private converse with learned men, a thing most long'd for by a Physitian that desireth chiefly to turn over the BOOK of NATURE
items.note: On his travels he had private converse with learned men, to whom he says he would hardly have been admitted but for the Relation he was then in.

items.quote: the BOOK of NATURE (in which every region is a leaf) not profunctorily & superficially, but practically and experimentally
items.note: The text says how its BOOK of NATURE is meant: every region is a leaf of it, and it is to be turned over practically and experimentally.

items.quote: Heroick Prince CHRISTIAN ANHALTIN, with his more then singular favor and laudable patronage toward the more secret Studies, supplyed me with necessary expences
items.note: Croll names his patron, who paid the necessary expenses out of favour toward the more secret Studies; he sets him down as a pattern for other great men to imitate.

items.quote: so great a burden as all these Medicins come to, which must be prepar'd and try'd by Fire
items.note: The medicines must be prepared and tried by Fire, at a cost Croll says he could not bear alone. Nothing more of the work is given in these lines.

items.quote: By which singular care toward the whole Spagyrick state
items.note: The text names a Spagyrick state toward which the patron's care is shown; later in the paragraph it speaks of citizens of the Physicall & Spagyrick State and profession.

items.quote: in respect of what concerns the order and Disposition of medicaments, I have proposed and set down this to my selfe
items.note: Croll speaks of an order and disposition of medicaments that he has set down after his own judgement; the lines given do not show where that ordered matter stands.

items.quote: It will be safe for every man to add hereunto the further Experiences of his own, and dispose it otherwise according to his discretion for his private use when he hath inlarg'd it
items.note: Every man may add his own experiences and order the matter otherwise for his private use.

items.quote: this harvest of Chymicall Corn, and the First fruits of my increase, and this Spagyrick present of my difficult and laborious diligence
items.what: this harvest of Chymicall Corn, and the First fruits of my increase, and this Spagyrick present
items.note: Three names Croll gives his work, which he thinks the best thing he could leave to his Country and Common-wealth.

items.quote: will be most acceptable to godly learned men (for I regard not Hogs & Dogs that have no grace nor goodnes at all, those Beetles which I leave to their own dunghil)
items.note: The work is meant for godly learned men; others, called Hogs, Dogs and Beetles, he does not regard.

items.quote: who have been train'd up in the Spagyrick and Hermetick School of Vulcan, being not yet deprived of the Light of understanding, and have been well instructed by approved Authors in the general rules of Physitians before observed
items.note: The readers it suits most of all: those trained in the Spagyrick and Hermetick School of Vulcan and taught by approved Authors in the general rules of Physitians. 'before observed' may point back to an earlier place; the lines given do not show it.

items.quote: I have not handled all things here in this place, to avoyd prolixity; I know there are not a few doubts left unresolved
items.note: Croll says he has not handled everything here and that doubts are left unresolved; the reason he gives is to avoid length.

items.quote: I have not spoken of so many things, but there yet more left to be spaken.
items.note: The margin note says more is left to be spoken than has been spoken.

items.quote: These things are writen for them who by aprospicocious & happy wit have their mind inlightned by God & their Soul seasoned with the salt of Wisdome.
items.note: The margin note says for whom these things are written: those whose mind God has enlightened and whose soul is seasoned with the salt of Wisdome.

items.quote: A few things or words are sufficient for him that understandeth.
items.note: The margin note says few words suffice the one who understands: the reader is to take more than is said.

items.quote: It is provided for by the Philosophical law that some tedious things should be left obscure to young Schollers and for intelligent & wise men to find out
items.note: By a Philosophical law some things are left obscure on purpose, for the wise to find out; the text adds that wits are thereby tried and made fit for the School of Phylosophers.

items.quote: He that can receive it let him receive it; and he that doth not understand, let him either learn or hold his peace and be silent
items.note: The text is for the one who can receive it; whoever does not understand is to learn or be silent.

items.quote: the young Pupil that is a diligent Searcher out of the Ancient First & Sacred Phylosophy
items.note: The philosophy the pupil searches out is named Ancient, First and Sacred; the pupil is to fear God, lay aside his Phantasie and have his Reason well disposed.

items.quote: he may apprehend & conjecture the signification of MANY things by a Few in this open market of Nature, not by a vulgar sharpsightednes but by the assistance of the Almighty
items.note: The text says a few things signify many, which the fit pupil may conjecture with God's help and not by common sharpness: a sign that what is written here stands for more than it says.

items.quote: shall at last with great thankfulnes acknowledge that the doors and Inner rooms are unlockt to him by the favorable virtue of the most high Creator
items.note: To the one who reads sincerely and examines inwardly, doors and Inner rooms are unlocked by the Creator's virtue: there is an inside that opens to some readers only.

items.quote: from all these things rightly understood, through PRAYER & PAINS, shall reap much more fruit than he expected
items.note: Rightly understood, through PRAYER and PAINS, these things yield more fruit than the reader expected.

items.quote: reproaching them for a patch'd and mixt hodg podg of good & bad together
items.name: any of a contrary opinion
items.note: A reproach Croll foresees from those of a contrary opinion and rejects: that such labours are a patched mixture of good and bad. He likens their censures to Aesop's Crow and their temper to Timon that Man-hater.

items.quote: to get the corn from the chaffe, and separate true from false, is sometime a most tedious and difficult task
items.note: Separating true from false is at times a tedious and difficult task, which he leaves to be judged by those who have toiled at the like.

items.quote: who (as already before) are justly to be casheer'd
items.note: The words 'as already before' point back to an earlier place in this writing where such opponents were dismissed; the lines given do not show it.

items.quote: let them open their own fountains, having an occasion given them hereby of publishing their Observations, let them take their lited candle from under the bushel, lest the curse of the figtree befall them
items.note: Those who would discourage others are told to publish their own observations.

items.name: Mat.
items.note: The margin note names a place in a writing beside the words on the curse of the figtree.

items.quote: a cunning & contentious Sceptick Phylosopher is inclin'd unto, whose purpose is not to find out that which is True but to wrangle about it
items.note: Croll sets aside contentions of words, Scholastick questions and fruitless disputations as the way of a Sceptick Phylosopher, who seeks wrangling and not what is true.

items.quote: to bring forth better things than these out of their own experience
items.note: Others are to be spurred by his example, as good citizens of the Physicall & Spagyrick State and profession, to bring out better things from their own experience.

items.quote: For who can find out the end of Physick.
items.note: The margin note says no one can find the end of Physick.

items.quote: for surely Physick is not yet come to the Limit of perfection, but many things remain to be discovered to future ages
items.note: Physick is not yet perfect; much remains for future ages to discover.

items.quote: to succor poor Lazarus, not wth Sylogistical or Levitical Words, but with a Samaritan Help & Ayd
items.note: The sick are to be helped with deeds and not with words; the text says so through the figures of Lazarus, Levitical words and Samaritan help.

items.quote: cast away the Signatures of cursed Sloth, of Drones, in their hollow cracks and clamors which at least make a terrible noyse, they may become Bees
items.note: Drones and Bees are used in a second sense for the idle, noisy opponents and for those who work; the text marks sloth and noise as the Signatures of Drones.

items.quote: conspire together with us into an union and Spagyrick mellifice divorcing the multitude and abstaining from all fornication
items.note: Following the Bees figure, the joint work is called a Spagyrick mellifice. 'fornication' and 'divorcing the multitude' stand in a passage about agreement in work, not about bodies. Interpreted (my inference, the narrowest): the words are used figuratively for keeping apart from the crowd and from mixing with what is foreign to the union; the text does not itself say what they mean.

items.quote: Really & indeed may maintain & defend the Excellency of Chymistry against all that reproach it
items.note: Those who join are to defend the Excellency of Chymistry against its reproachers and to better his endeavour without envy.

items.quote: after other secret Sciences which yet lie in the dark
items.note: Other secret Sciences are said still to lie in the dark.

items.quote: that Ancient, True, & Philosophical Medicin, which by reason of the long continuance and injury of time, as also the unworthines of our age (mens sins doubtles so meeting together) is not yet fully known
items.note: The Medicine is named Ancient, True and Philosophical, and is said to be not yet fully known, through the injury of time and the unworthiness of the age.

items.quote: be restored to its lost lustre & ancient splendor, to the most healthful advantage of all man kind & the due honor of Spagyrick Phisitians
items.note: Croll expects that this Medicine may in a short time, by heavenly help, be restored to its ancient splendour, for the good of mankind and the honour of Spagyrick Phisitians.

items.quote: whose endeavor & pains that immense sea of divine Mercy would be pleased to make use of as an Instrument & Pen to accomplish so healthful and saving a work
items.note: The Spagyrick physicians' pains are wished to be God's Instrument and Pen for this work.

items.quote: it concerns the publick good to make known also in publick writing what belongs to the publick
items.note: Here what belongs to the public is to be made known in public writing; CH6.71 says the most secret of secrets have ever been hid from the common sort, and this same paragraph says some things are left obscure by the Philosophical law and that he imparted only so far as was lawful. The lines given do not say where the line between the two is drawn.

items.quote: Which that holy Triunity grant, whose unspeakable Name be blessed for ever and ever
items.note: The writing closes with a prayer that the holy Triunity grant what the last paragraph hopes for: the restoring of the Medicine.

items.quote: AMEN.
items.note: The last word of the text given; the prayer and the Preface's conclusion end here.
